items.readable_text:
Content:
The line integral with respect to [MATH: x] of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] along the path [MATH: C] can be calculated using the formula

Content:
[MATH: \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t,]
where [MATH: \mathbf r (t)] for [MATH: a\leq t\leq b] is a parametrization of [MATH: C.]

Content:
Now, if we set [MATH: f(x,y) = 1,] then by the change of variables formula, we have

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{C}dx|= ∫_(a)^(b)(dx)/(dt)dt; = ∫_(x_{1})^(x_{2})dx; = x_{2} − x_{1},]

Content:
where [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] are the [MATH: x]-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of [MATH: C,] respectively. To summarize,

Content:
[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1.]

Content:
Let's use this result to calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d x,] where [MATH: C] is the path along the quarter-circle of radius [MATH: 2] centered at [MATH: O] in the first quadrant, traversed in the clockwise direction, as shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1869e2ffb99b71bc6f3193219081fca4]

Content:
The initial point is [MATH: (0,2)] and the terminal point is [MATH: (2,0).] So, we have [MATH: x_1 = 0, x_2 = 2,] and therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = 2-0 = 2.]

[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1 = (-3) - 3 = -6.]

Earlier, we showed that
[MATH: \int_{C}\,\textrm d x = 2,]

Content:
The initial and terminal points have swapped, and so we now have [MATH: x_1 = 2] and [MATH: x_2 = 0.] Applying our formula, we have
[MATH: ∫_{− C}dx|= x_{2} − x_{1}; = 0 − 2; = − 2.]

Content:
> Let [MATH: C] be a piecewise-smooth path in the [MATH: xy]-plane, and let [MATH: -C] be the curve consisting of the same points as [MATH: C] but with the opposite orientation. Then,
> [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.]
> Similarly,
> [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d y = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d y.]

Content:
In other words, line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are dependent on orientation. This is quite different from the case for line integrals with respect to arc length, which are independent of orientation.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2] be a piecewise smooth path in the [MATH: xy]-plane, and let [MATH: -C] be the curve consisting of the same points as [MATH: C] but with the opposite orientation.

For line integrals with respect to [MATH: x,] we have the following properties:

  • [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x]

  • [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x + \int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x]

In our case, we have:

[MATH: ∫_{C}f(x, y)dx|= ∫_{C_{1}}f(x, y)dx + ∫_{C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 8|= − ∫_{− C_{1}}f(x, y)dx − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 8|= − (− 2) − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 8|= 2 − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 6|= − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx]

Therefore,

[MATH: \int_{-C_2} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x = -6.]

If [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x= 8] and [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C_1} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x= -2,] calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C_2} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x] given that [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Let [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2] be a piecewise smooth path in the [MATH: xy]-plane, and let [MATH: -C] be the curve consisting of the same points as [MATH: C] but with the opposite orientation.

For line integrals with respect to [MATH: x,] we have the following properties:

- [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x]
- [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x + \int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x]

In our case, we have:

[MATH: ∫_{C}f(x, y)dx|= ∫_{C_{1}}f(x, y)dx + ∫_{C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 8|= − ∫_{− C_{1}}f(x, y)dx − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 8|= − (− 2) − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 8|= 2 − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx; 6|= − ∫_{− C_{2}}f(x, y)dx]

Therefore,

[MATH: \int_{-C_2} f(x,y) \,\textrm d x = -6.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
The line integral with respect to [MATH: x] of the function [MATH: f(x,y)] along the path [MATH: C] can be calculated using the formula

Content:
[MATH: \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int\limits_a^b f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \dfrac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \, \textrm{d}t,]
where [MATH: \mathbf r (t)] for [MATH: a\leq t\leq b] is a parametrization of [MATH: C.]

Content:
Now, if we set [MATH: f(x,y) = 1,] then by the change of variables formula, we have

Content:
[MATH: ∫_{C}dx|= ∫_(a)^(b)(dx)/(dt)dt; = ∫_(x_{1})^(x_{2})dx; = x_{2} − x_{1},]

Content:
where [MATH: x_1] and [MATH: x_2] are the [MATH: x]-coordinates at the initial and terminal points of [MATH: C,] respectively. To summarize,

Content:
[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1.]

Content:
Let's use this result to calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\int_C\,\textrm d x,] where [MATH: C] is the path along the quarter-circle of radius [MATH: 2] centered at [MATH: O] in the first quadrant, traversed in the clockwise direction, as shown below:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1869e2ffb99b71bc6f3193219081fca4]

Content:
The initial point is [MATH: (0,2)] and the terminal point is [MATH: (2,0).] So, we have [MATH: x_1 = 0, x_2 = 2,] and therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = 2-0 = 2.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Some Remarks

Content:
In addition, we note the following regarding line integrals with respect to [MATH: x\mathbin{:}]

Content:
- If [MATH: C = C_1\cup C_2] is a piecewise-smooth curve, then
[MATH: \int_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = \int_{C_1} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x + \int_{C_2} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.]
- When [MATH: C] is a closed curve, we sometimes use the following notation:
[MATH: \oint_C f(x,y)\,\textrm d x]
If the curve is traversed once, the initial and terminal points are the same, so [MATH: x_1 = x_2.] Therefore, for line integrals of unity with respect to [MATH: x,] we have
[MATH: \oint_C \,\textrm d x = 0.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Line Integrals of Unity With Respect to X

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle\int_C \,\textrm d x,] where [MATH: C=C_1 \cup C_2] is the path comprising of two line segments, as shown below.

[IMG: /graphics/8e812447b89c4e3aa73cf9f3313ab5fc]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The line integral of unity with respect to [MATH: x] along a path [MATH: C] is equal to the net change in [MATH: x] between the terminal and initial points:

[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1,]
where [MATH: x_2] is the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the terminal point, and [MATH: x_1] is the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, [MATH: x_2 = -3] and [MATH: x_1 = 3.] Therefore,

[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d x = x_2 - x_1 = (-3) - 3 = -6.]

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Line Integrals of Unity With Respect to Y

Content:
Similar to line integrals of unity with respect to [MATH: x,] the line integral of unity with respect to [MATH: y] along a path [MATH: C] is equal to the net change in [MATH: y] between the terminal and initial points:
[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d y = y_2 - y_1,]
where [MATH: y_2] is the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the terminal point, and [MATH: y_1] is the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the initial point.

Content:
Also, if [MATH: C] is a closed, positively oriented curve traversed once in the counterclockwise direction, then

Content:
[MATH: \oint_C \,\textrm d y = 0.]

---

[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d y = y_2 - y_1,]
where [MATH: y_2] is the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the terminal point, and [MATH: y_1] is the [MATH: y]-coordinate of the initial point.

In our case, [MATH: y_2 = 0] and [MATH: y_1 = 0.] Therefore,

[MATH: \int_C \,\textrm d y = y_2 - y_1 = 0 - 0 = 0.]

Item 10 — Tutorial: Further Properties of Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y

Content:
Earlier, we showed that
[MATH: \int_{C}\,\textrm d x = 2,]
where [MATH: C] is the path along the quarter-circle shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/a1091b66483bbac0be985dfaf90352ba]

Content:
If we reverse the orientation of the curve, we get the following path:

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/ef1d61242efb6f381c8be7c95f380fac]

Content:
The initial and terminal points have swapped, and so we now have [MATH: x_1 = 2] and [MATH: x_2 = 0.] Applying our formula, we have
[MATH: ∫_{− C}dx|= x_{2} − x_{1}; = 0 − 2; = − 2.]
This example illustrates an important property of line integrals with respect to [MATH: x,] described in full as follows:

Content:
> Let [MATH: C] be a piecewise-smooth path in the [MATH: xy]-plane, and let [MATH: -C] be the curve consisting of the same points as [MATH: C] but with the opposite orientation. Then,
> [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d x.]
> Similarly,
> [MATH: \displaystyle\int_{-C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d y = -\int_{C} f(x,y)\,\textrm d y.]

Content:
In other words, line integrals with respect to [MATH: x] and [MATH: y] are dependent on orientation. This is quite different from the case for line integrals with respect to arc length, which are independent of orientation.

---
